title: Can a word be its own opposite? | CONTRONYMS

entries.note: A word that is its own opposite, often requested by listeners; also called [[see:antagonym]], [[see:auto-antonym]], [[see:enantionym]] or [[see:Janus words]].
Another name for a [[see:contronym]].
Another name for a [[see:contronym]].
Another name for a [[see:contronym]], meaning opposite name in Greek.
Another name for contronyms, named after [[from:Janus]], the two-faced Roman god, because these words are two-faced.
Named after [[from:Janus]], in theory because the first month looks back at the past year and forward to the next.
Some contronyms are homonyms: words from two different etymological sources that are spelled the same, like [[see:cleave]].
Means both to split and to cling, from two similar Old English verbs; the sticky one relates to [[same-root:clay]], the splitting one to [[same-root:clever]].
Shares a Proto-Indo-European root with the sticking sense of [[same-root:cleave]].
Shares a root with the splitting sense of [[same-root:cleave]]; originally referred to manual dexterity rather than intellect.
Can mean to sprinkle dust on or brush it off, because the noun came first and the verb covered many things done with dust.
Rob's packet of shelled pistachios could mean either with shells on or with shells removed.
Means both to permit and to prohibit, from Latin [[from:sancire]], to render sacred, hence to make law; related to [[same-root:sanctify]] and [[same-root:saint]].
Shares its origin with [[same-root:sanction]].
Arguably shares its holy origin with [[same-root:sanction]].
Means both swift and firmly attached, from an Old English sense of vigorous or strong; [[see:Anglish]] uses it for castle.
A way of speaking that avoids borrowings, especially Romance ones; it uses [[see:fast]] for castle.
An Old English compound Jess likes, showing the firm sense of [[see:fast]].
First meant filling you with awe, mostly positive until the 1800s, so today a time can be awful or awfully good; an example of [[see:semantic bleaching]].
When a word is used so much it loses its power, as with [[see:awful]], [[see:awesome]] and [[see:terrific]].
Another word, like [[see:awful]], that once meant something profound and has weakened.
Another word, like [[see:awful]], that once meant something profound in the opposite direction.
When a word that implied something bad becomes good; ameliorate comes from French [[from:améliorer]], to improve; the opposite of [[see:pejoration]].
When a word that was initially good goes bad, as in [[same-root:pejorative]]; the opposite of [[see:amelioration]].
Given as related to [[same-root:pejoration]].
Originally to read carefully in detail, now also a casual browse; an example of [[see:semantic broadening]], and arguably [[see:skunked]].
When a word gains a new meaning while keeping the old one, as with [[see:peruse]].
Said of a word misused until it is no longer useful, discussed in an earlier episode; [[see:peruse]] is probably one.
To table an idea means putting it forward in British usage but setting it aside in American business usage.
A contested word used since the 1870s and in all major dictionaries, probably a blend of [[from:regardless]] and [[from:irrespective]].
Thought to have blended with [[see:irrespective]] to give [[gave:irregardless]].
Thought to have blended with [[see:regardless]] to give [[gave:irregardless]].
To screen something can mean hiding it, but screening a film means showing it.
Both an admission of error and a formal defence, as in literary apologies like [[see:Plato's Apology]]; the defence sense survives in [[see:apologist]].
An example of the defence sense of [[see:apology]].
Someone who defends a stance rather than says sorry, keeping the old defence sense of [[same-root:apology]].
Older than [[see:flammable]], it means able to be [[see:inflamed]], i.e. set alight; its confusing look led to the shortened form.
Used to mean set alight, which explains the sense of [[see:inflammable]].
Shortened from [[from:inflammable]] for clarity, presumably during the Industrial Revolution when goods were being labelled.
An oversight committee pays close attention, yet committing an oversight means overlooking something; [[see:overlook]] is arguably another contronym.
Suggested as another contronym, like [[see:oversight]].
The name for people from a place, coined in its current sense around 1990, from Greek [[from:demos]]; in the 1890s it meant someone named after a place, or a pen name.
Rob wrongly believed [[see:demonym]] was invented for Wikipedia, where it appears in every place's sidebar.
Shares the Greek root demos with [[same-root:demonym]].
What people in Massachusetts call themselves.
What people from Salem, Massachusetts call themselves; Jess is unsure of the pronunciation.
Someone from Manchester, from [[from:Mancunium]], the Roman name for Manchester.
Someone from Cambridge, from [[from:Cantabrigia]], the Roman name for the city.
Its name may have shifted because the Normans struggled to pronounce the earlier form, after which the river was renamed the [[see:Cam]].
The river through Cambridge, formerly called the [[see:Granta]]; it was renamed to match the town's Norman-altered name.
A lesser-known name for someone from Leeds, from [[from:Loidis]], the Roman name for Leeds.
A satisfying state demonym, for someone from Michigan, that still makes sense to outsiders.
A satisfying state demonym, for someone from Arkansas, that still makes sense to outsiders.
Someone from Maine, who can also be a [[see:Maniac]].
Someone from Michigan's Upper Peninsula.
Reportedly used for people from Michigan's Lower Peninsula because they live under the bridge.
Someone from Wisconsin, a big cheese producer; [[see:Green Bay Packers]] fans wear cheese-shaped hats in honour of the state.
Wisconsin football team named after a meat-packing company, whose fans wear cheese hats in honour of the state.
Someone from Illinois, named for how flat the state is.
A possibly offensive Rhode Island demonym, though listed on the official state page.
An alternative to [[see:Mainer]] for someone from Maine, which Jess finds perfect.
Oklahoma demonym made somewhat pejorative during the Dust Bowl, as portrayed in [[see:The Grapes of Wrath]].
Oklahoma demonym, originally negative, for settlers who illegally entered the unassigned lands before the official land rush, unlike the [[see:Boomer]]s.
Name for participants in the officially sanctioned Oklahoma land rush, linked with a pioneering spirit, in contrast to [[see:Sooner]]s.
John Steinbeck's novel, where you can read about the Dust Bowl era when [[see:Okie]] became pejorative.
Delaware demonym, possibly apocryphally after [[from?:Captain Caldwell]] of Kent County, who carried a pair of fighting gamecocks.
Delaware demonym, apparently from the many muskrats present in the state's early days.
New Yorker descended from Dutch settlers, also referring to the trousers, popularised by Washington Irving's satirical character [[see:Diedrich Knickerbocker]].
A satirical character in Washington Irving's hoax stories who popularised [[see:Knickerbocker]].
A name for someone from Liverpool, also called a [[see:Scouser]].
Someone from Liverpool, named after [[from:lobscouse]], a stew popular with sailors.
A meat and vegetable stew popular with sailors, also called scouse, which gave [[gave:Scouser]].
Someone from Newcastle, from the northern English and Scottish pet form of George, a popular name among the city's miners and sailors.
The name for people from Birmingham.
Someone born within the sound of [[see:Bow Bells]], most likely from [[from?:cokeney]], a cock's egg, unkindly applied to city dwellers; possibly from French [[from?:coquin]].
The bells of Bow church; to be a [[see:Cockney]] you must in theory be born within their sound.
Since a cock can't lay eggs, it meant dodgy offspring like a petulant child or runt; it is the leading theory for [[gave?:Cockney]].
French word used to describe a cheeky child, a less favoured possible source of [[gave?:Cockney]].
Someone from Connecticut, the Nutmeg State, possibly from Yankee pedlars selling counterfeit wooden nutmegs in colonial times, though that may be apocryphal.
A Germanic-style demonym for a country with a Germanic name, contrasted with Latinate ones like [[see:Mauritian]].
A Latinate demonym for a Latinate country name, contrasted with [[see:Icelander]].
An example of dropping -land from a country named after a tribe.
The tribe behind England's name, though people from England aren't called Angles.
Jess's only guess for the English demonym; it isn't fit for purpose because it includes the Scots and Welsh, and England has no real demonym.
With Englishwoman, the tempting term for someone from England, which Rob doubts will last.
Calling one person from Switzerland a Swiss just doesn't feel right to Rob.
Doesn't seem to follow the usual rules, but comes from Old French [[from:Espaignart]].
The name of an ethnic group, as opposed to a [[see:demonym]] for people of a place; e.g. [[see:Kazakh]] versus [[see:Kazakhstani]].
An ethnonym for someone who probably, but not necessarily, lives in Kazakhstan, unlike [[see:Kazakhstani]].
The demonym for someone from Kazakhstan, contrasted with the ethnonym [[see:Kazakh]].
The ethnonym, contrasted with the demonym [[see:Croatian]].
The demonym, contrasted with the ethnonym [[see:Croat]].
Anything named after a person or proper noun, like [[see:Vanderbilt University]] or an eponymous album.
Named after [[from:Cornelius Vanderbilt]], an example of an [[see:eponym]].
From Civil War general [[from:Ambrose Burnside]]'s whiskers; its parts were swapped once the link was forgotten, which upset [[see:Ambrose Bierce]].
Rob counts [[see:sideburns]] as a non-standard folk etymology, switching parts around rather than substituting them.
Blacklisted [[see:sideburns]] in his 1909 book Write It Right, upset that the link to Burnside was lost.
A deliberate political lie, from the fictional [[from:Baron von Roorback]], supposed source of an 1844 rumour about [[see:James K. Polk]].
The 11th president, falsely rumoured in 1844 to have branded his slaves with his initials, giving rise to [[see:roorback]].
Made-up source of the Polk rumour, who gave [[gave:roorback]].
An example of 1800s fictional characters who became emblematic of groups, like [[see:Baron von Roorback]].
Political cartoons illustrated carpetbaggers as characters in the post-Civil War era.
A traitor, after [[from:Vidkun Quisling]], the Norwegian who helped the Germans invade Norway.
For a while synonymous with treachery in the US, like [[see:quisling]].
From possibly fictional [[from:Nicolas Chauvin]]; first fanatical nationalistic zeal, it became tied to male chauvinism through 1960s feminism and now approaches misogyny.
Possibly fictional figure emblematic of Napoleonic zeal, the name being common in that group; he gave [[gave:chauvinist]].
A genericised trademark, where a brand name replaces the name of the thing, like [[see:Kleenex]] or [[see:Band-Aid]].
Used in the US instead of tissues, a [[see:proprietary eponym]].
Used in the US for an adhesive bandage, which the British call a [[see:plaster]].
British for a [[see:Band-Aid]]; Rob doesn't know why, perhaps because it's a sticking plaster or a mini cast.
A big British proprietary eponym, as in doing the hoovering; in the US it would suggest the president or J. Edgar Hoover.
Still a trademark owned by Parker Brothers; originally [[see:table tennis]] or [[see:whiff-whaff]].
The original name for what became known as [[see:ping pong]].
A good old name for [[see:table tennis]], which Jess guesses is onomatopoeic.
Originally a trademark, now generic.
Originally a trademark, now generic.
Originally a trademark, now generic.
Originally a trademark, now generic.
Originally a trademark, now generic.
Originally a trademark; Rob would call his trouser zip his [[see:fly]], though zipper suits the technology better.
Originally a trademark, now generic.
Rob's word for the [[see:zipper]] on trousers, which Jess finds an odd choice.
A stun gun; an acronym inspired by [[see:laser]] but standing for Tom A. Swift's Electric Rifle, after [[from:Tom Swift and His Electric Rifle]].
Largely inspired the form of [[see:taser]], though the letters stand for nothing in common.
A teenage genius inventor in [[see:Edward Stratemeyer]]'s syndicate books whose electric rifle inspired the [[see:taser]].
His syndicate published Tom Swift, the Hardy Boys and Nancy Drew, often by ghostwriters; he reportedly wrote about 1,300 himself.

entries.term: Tom Swift and His Electric Rifle
entries.note: Also called Daring Adventures in Elephant Land; involves killing many elephants and native people, with offensive language, and inspired the [[gave:taser]].
Not -nym but -onym, from Greek [[from:onoma]], name, also found at the start of [[same-root:onomatopoeia]].
Disappointingly means named in this way; The Liar's Dictionary defines it as the sound of trying to spell it on a keyboard.
A real person's name used by an author without permission to suggest someone else wrote a work, like signing a bad play as Shakespeare.
A name based on someone's characteristics, like the Seven Dwarves or Chaucer's [[see:Placebo]].
A sycophantic character in Chaucer whose name means I am to please, an example of a [[see:charactonym]].
A name apt for its bearer, like [[see:Usain Bolt]], a tighter term than [[see:nominative determinism]].
A clunky phrase associated with [[see:aptronym]]s, which Rob is glad now has a shorter word.
One of the world's fastest people, an [[see:aptronym]].
A classic [[see:aptronym]].
A psychiatrist with an [[see:aptronym]].
Starbucks executive who also worked for Molson Coors Brewing Company, an [[see:aptronym]].
Former head of the nonprofit Food for the Poor, corrected from aptronym to [[see:inaptronym]] since he provided food.
The TV weather presenter where Rob grew up, an [[see:aptronym]].
A name implying the opposite of what the person does, like [[see:Robin Mahfood]]; also called a [[see:caconym]].
An inappropriate name, sharing its first element with [[same-root:cacophony]], a bad sound; contrasted with [[see:euonym]].
A bad sound, used to explain the first element of [[same-root:caconym]].
A beautiful-sounding instrument, used to explain the first element of [[same-root:euonym]].
A nice, well-suited name, like a pretty woman called Rose; close to an [[see:aptronym]].
Addressed before; he didn't invent the toilet but worked in sanitation, so had an [[see:aptronym]].
A repetitive name, like [[see:Torpenhow Hill]]; specifically a zoological name with identical genus and species, like [[see:Rattus rattus]], banned in botany.
Jess's example of a repetitive name, meaning the tar tar pits.
An English place whose name means hill hill hill, an example of a repetitive name.
The rat, a zoological [[see:tautonym]].
A zoological [[see:tautonym]].
Offered as an example of a [[see:tautonym]].
A zoological [[see:tautonym]].
A new term for an old thing, needed after an advance; retro means backwards; coined by NPR president [[see:Frank Mankiewicz]].
A [[see:retronym]]: all diapers were cloth until disposable ones were invented.
A [[see:retronym]]: satellite meant any natural orbiting object until Sputnik was launched.
A [[see:retronym]] once just called a guitar, now contrasted with the electric guitar.
A [[see:retronym]] needed within a few decades once the mobile telephone arrived.
A [[see:retronym]] distinguishing it from ebooks and audiobooks.
A [[see:retronym]].
A [[see:retronym]].
A [[see:retronym]].
A [[see:retronym]]: the first PlayStation was re-released as the PS1 after the PS2 came out.
A [[see:retronym]]: what was the Great War had to be renamed the First World War.
A [[see:retronym]]: name a child after yourself and you become Senior or the First.
